sections.heading: History and contemporary trends
sections.detailed: Cognitive psychology studies how information is represented, transformed and used. Introspection and early experimental work preceded behaviourism; limitations of stimulus–response accounts helped motivate the cognitive revolution. Information processing introduced representations, stages and limited capacity. Contemporary work links behavioural experiments with computational models and neuroscience. Artificial intelligence models can test whether a proposed mechanism reproduces behaviour, but matching performance does not prove that humans use the same mechanism. Robotic systems combine sensing, action and feedback; embodied approaches ask how cognition depends on the body and environment.

sections.heading: Research methods: strengths and limitations

Reaction-time and accuracy tasks infer processing indirectly and can show speed–accuracy trade-offs. Case studies reveal selective impairments but generalisation and premorbid differences are concerns. Computational modelling makes assumptions explicit, although different models can fit the same data. sections.heading: Cognitive neuropsychology
sections.detailed: Cognitive neuropsychology uses patterns of impaired and preserved performance after brain damage to test theories of normal cognition. A single dissociation occurs when one task is impaired while another is relatively preserved; different task difficulty can explain it. A double dissociation reverses the pattern across patients or conditions and more strongly supports separable processes. Interpretation still depends on assumptions about modularity, compensatory strategies and lesion distribution. A lesion rarely removes one isolated function, so combine patient evidence with behavioural and neural findings.

sections.heading: Attention: types and influencing factors
sections.detailed: Selective attention prioritises some information; divided attention distributes resources across tasks; sustained attention maintains readiness over time. Orienting may be voluntary and goal-directed or captured by salient events. Alertness, fatigue, arousal, motivation, task difficulty, practice and stimulus salience influence performance. Dual-task costs depend on shared resources and response demands, not simply the number of activities. In an exam, distinguish attention type from the factors that influence it and describe an appropriate experimental measure.

sections.heading: Bottleneck theories and Broadbent’s filter
sections.detailed: Bottleneck theories propose a capacity-limited stage that prevents all input from receiving equivalent processing. Broadbent proposed early selection based on physical characteristics, with selected input reaching a limited-capacity channel. Dichotic listening and shadowing support selective processing, but personally meaningful unattended information challenges a rigid all-or-none filter. Attenuation accounts allow weakened unattended input to reach meaning under some conditions; late-selection accounts place selection after semantic analysis. Compare models by selection location, unattended processing and the evidence each explains.

sections.heading: Automatic versus controlled processing
sections.detailed: Controlled processing typically requires intention, attention and flexible task management, making it vulnerable to competing demands. Automatic processing can become fast and relatively low-effort through practice but may be difficult to suppress. Automaticity is a collection of properties rather than a universal all-or-none category. In the Stroop task, habitual word reading interferes with naming ink colour, illustrating conflict between task goals and a well-practised response. Consistent mapping promotes automaticity; changed rules can expose inflexibility and interference.

sections.heading: Object recognition: template, prototype and feature models
sections.detailed: Template matching compares an input with stored patterns, but size, rotation and viewpoint variation require many templates or transformations. Prototype models compare input with an abstract typical representation and can explain graded category membership. Distinctive-feature models identify diagnostic components; shared features explain some confusions. Recognition-by-components describes objects using arrangements of simpler volumetric parts. Computational approaches specify algorithms and representations, including distributed networks. Evaluate each model against invariance, unfamiliar views, context effects and errors rather than presenting them as interchangeable labels.

sections.heading: Bottom-up and top-down perception
sections.detailed: Bottom-up processing builds a percept from sensory evidence; top-down processing uses knowledge, expectations and context to interpret that evidence. Ambiguous letters are easier to identify in familiar words, but expectations can also produce misperceptions. Most perception involves interaction: data constrain candidate interpretations while prior knowledge guides attention and interpretation. A useful experiment manipulates context while holding a target constant. Avoid claiming that top-down processing creates arbitrary perceptions independent of sensory input.

sections.heading: Memory models, STM and working memory
sections.detailed: The modal model distinguishes sensory registers, short-term storage and long-term memory, with control processes such as rehearsal. Short-term memory concerns temporary retention; working memory includes manipulation and coordination. Baddeley’s model distinguishes a central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad and episodic buffer. Dual-task interference can reveal partly separable resources. Capacity depends on material, chunking, knowledge and task demands, so a single digit-span estimate is not a universal measure. Levels-of-processing accounts emphasise encoding operations rather than separate stores alone.

sections.heading: Long-term memory systems
sections.detailed: Episodic memory concerns personally experienced events with temporal and spatial context; semantic memory concerns general knowledge. Procedural memory supports skills and habits and may be expressed without conscious recollection. These distinctions do not mean every memory belongs to one completely isolated box: systems interact during learning and retrieval. sections.heading: Psycholinguistics, history and Chomsky’s approach
sections.detailed: Psycholinguistics studies the mental processes involved in acquiring, understanding and producing language. Chomsky challenged accounts based only on reinforcement and proposed that linguistic competence requires structured grammatical knowledge. Generative grammar emphasises rules capable of generating novel sentences. Distinguish competence from performance limitations such as attention and memory. Critiques question strong innate specificity and insufficient attention to meaning, usage, interaction and learning. Contemporary accounts compare predictions about acquisition, processing and neural implementation rather than treating one historical theory as a complete explanation.
